beats.narration_text: In June of 2025, a 1970s folk-country quartet called Velvet Sundown appeared on Spotify. Gabe Farrow on vocals, Lennie West on guitar, Milo Rains on bass, Orion Del Mar on drums. Within four weeks: nine hundred thousand monthly listeners. There was just one problem. None of them exist.

shot.title: The band that doesn't exist
shot.dek: Nine hundred thousand listeners. Zero humans.

beats.narration_text: This is a film about ghost artists and real ones. Not about whether AI music is good or bad — about what happens when the machine that decides what you hear can be captured for forty dollars. And about why the real fraud was never in the music. It was in the graph.

shot.title: The pitch
shot.dek: The fraud is in the graph.

beats.narration_text: Here is the anatomy. Velvet Sundown's entire operation cost its creators less than forty dollars in subscription fees, and took under an hour to produce its core assets. By mid-July a third album was out, and a single called Dust on the Wind had crossed two million streams. All of it generated by AI.

shot.title: Forty dollars and an hour
shot.dek: Under an hour. Under forty dollars.

beats.narration_text: Here is the part that should bother you. After the synthetic nature was confirmed — after everyone knew — the band stayed on Spotify. A third album was released after the reveal. Spotify declined to remove the content. The royalties kept flowing.

The industry has a vocabulary problem. There is a legal distinction between an artist who is synthetic and one who impersonates. Impersonation attaches to a real identity and feeds. Platforms built elaborate defenses against that. The synthetic artist creates from nothing — no host, no victim, no stolen face. The law has no word for it. So neither do the defenses.

shot.title: Two kinds of fake
shot.dek: No host. No victim. No word for it.

beats.narration_text: Spotify's recommendation engine does not measure music. It measures behavior. Not artistic merit, not cultural resonance — whether you save, whether you playlist, whether you play to completion, and above all, whether you skip. The skip rate is the death signal. Everything else is negotiable.

Velvet Sundown's operators understood this perfectly. During the critical two-to-four-week contamination window, aged bot accounts calibrated to the listening patterns of seventies folk enthusiasts discovered the debut. Save rates were tuned to sit within two standard deviations of genre averages. And the bots were programmed never to skip.

Then the cascade. By the time real humans met Velvet Sundown on Discover Weekly, the momentum was self-sustaining. A verified artist badge. Nine hundred thousand monthly listeners. Real people assumed legitimacy, saved the tracks, added them to playlists — and their genuine behavioral data flowed into the graph and reinforced what the bots had manufactured.

shot.title: The social proof cascade
shot.dek: The machine laundered fraud into taste.

beats.narration_text: This was not a novel fraud. It was an evolution. The prior generation — profile hijacking — needed a host, some niche act whose catalog got replaced through distributor exploits. The victim eventually noticed, and a takedown clock started. Synthetic artist construction needs no host and no victim. Hijacking is a smash-and-grab. This is a portfolio strategy.

And here is the detail that should keep you up at night. The operators described Velvet Sundown as a commissioned test — for a client interested in what they called psyop marketing. The test confirmed the discovery mechanisms can be fully captured within the platform's stated terms of service. It generated an estimated forty thousand dollars in gross royalties. Someone commissioned it. That someone has the results.

shot.title: The commissioned test
shot.dek: A commissioned test. Someone has the results.

beats.narration_text: The genre was not aesthetic. It was operational. Researchers describe genre entropy — how much listener behavior deviates from predictable patterns. Low-entropy genres like ambient, sleep, and acoustic have passive listeners with structurally low skip rates. Bot behavior is trivial to mimic there. And the genre's lo-fi production conveniently masks the watery artifacts of AI audio.

shot.title: Genre as a weapon
shot.dek: The genre was a tactical choice.

beats.narration_text: Before you blame the outsiders, know this: the platform normalized it first. One investigation found a composer named Johan Rohr who released over twenty-seven hundred songs under six hundred fifty-six aliases and captured fifteen billion streams — Spotify's own ghost artist program filling low-entropy playlists with anonymous, algorithmically optimized content. The difference between Rohr's network and Velvet Sundown is provenance, not method.

shot.title: The platform did it first
shot.dek: Fifteen billion streams. Six hundred fifty-six aliases.

beats.narration_text: Spotify's answer is SongDNA — digital liner notes tracing provenance, samples, collaborators. It catches impersonation. It catches voice cloning. Against synthetic artist construction, it is structurally blind. Velvet Sundown uses no samples and has no collaborators. In the system it looks like a new leaf with no connections — which is exactly what a genuinely new independent artist looks like.

shot.title: What SongDNA cannot see
shot.dek: Provenance tools can't see the graph.

beats.narration_text: None of this means AI music is fraud. Musinique's own constellation of ghost artists — Champa Jaan, Newton Williams Brown, Tuzi Brown, Mayfield King — is AI-assisted music with full disclosure, built around genuine human purpose. The AI is the production tool. The intent is human. Disclosure is the line. Synthetic is not the crime. Undisclosed manipulation of the graph is.

Researchers propose three structural responses. One: mandatory provenance — someone signs their name to AI-generated content and accepts accountability. Two: entropy analysis at the account level, detecting listening patterns too clean to be human, because humans skip and bots do not. Three: takedown rights for independent artists facing aesthetic theft, like the Breaking Rust case, where an AI project topped Billboard's country digital chart. And the industry is stirring — UMG is currently suing DistroKid over undisclosed AI music passed off as human-made.

The fraud was never in the music. The fraud was in the graph — in the system that decides what reaches your ears. Velvet Sundown is still on Spotify. The third album is still generating royalties. Until the platforms build a vocabulary for the contamination of the recommendation graph itself, this is not a violation of anything. It is a business model.

shot.title: The graph
shot.dek: Still on Spotify. Still a business model.
